questions.stem: Why is the hydrogen atom of HBr described as the electrophile?

options.text: It carries a delta-positive charge from the polarised bond
options.explanation: Bromine's higher electronegativity leaves hydrogen electron-poor.

options.text: It donates electrons to the alkene
options.explanation: The hydrogen accepts electron density - donation runs the other way.
The negative end of HBr is the bromine.
HBr adds by the ionic electrophilic route.

questions.stem: What happens to the polarised H-Br bond during step one of the mechanism?

options.text: It transfers its electrons to hydrogen
options.explanation: Hydrogen departs bonded to the pi pair instead.

options.text: It breaks heterolytically, both electrons leaving with bromine
options.explanation: The pair departs to the more electronegative atom.

options.text: It breaks homolytically to give radicals
options.explanation: No radicals appear in electrophilic addition.
The bromide must be free to attack in step two.

questions.stem: Which species attacks the carbocation in step two?

options.explanation: Hydrogen has already been delivered to the first carbon.
The bromide is the reagent's own partner.

options.text: The bromide ion with its lone pair
options.explanation: Br(-) donates a pair to the positive carbon.
One addition is complete after two steps.

questions.stem: Where must a curly arrow start in a valid mechanism?

options.explanation: Arrows follow electrons, never nuclei.
Charges mark destinations, not origins.
Origins must be electron sources - precision carries the mark.

options.text: From a bond or a lone pair of electrons
options.explanation: Arrows track electron pairs, so they begin where pairs live.

questions.stem: When the polarised HBr adds to propene, which product is the major one and why?

options.text: 2-bromopropane, via the more stable secondary carbocation
options.explanation: The positive charge sits on the middle carbon where alkyl groups steady it.

options.text: 1-bromopropane, via the more stable primary carbocation
options.explanation: Primary carbocations are the less stable kind.
No radical intermediates operate here.
The regioselectivity is decided, not random.

questions.stem: Define the term electrophile and identify it in the HBr addition.
questions.modelAnswer: An electrophile is an electron-pair acceptor attracted to electron-rich regions; in HBr addition the delta-positive hydrogen fills that role.

questions.stem: Write the two steps of the HBr-plus-ethene mechanism in words, in order.
questions.modelAnswer: First the pi bond attacks the delta-positive hydrogen while H-Br breaks to bromide, forming the carbocation; then the bromide ion donates its lone pair to the carbocation.

questions.stem: Explain why a carbocation intermediate forms in this mechanism.
questions.modelAnswer: Heterolytic fission hands the H-Br electron pair entirely to bromine, so after hydrogen bonds to one alkene carbon the other carbon is left electron-short and formally positive until bromide arrives.

questions.stem: Draw the full mechanism for HBr adding to ethene, marking both curly arrow origins.
questions.modelAnswer: Arrow one runs from the C=C pi bond to the delta-positive hydrogen, arrow two runs from the H-Br bond to bromine giving Br(-); after the carbocation appears, arrow three runs from the Br(-) lone pair onto the positive carbon.

questions.stem: What polarises the Br-Br bond as bromine approaches an alkene?

options.explanation: Light initiates radical reactions, not this ionic addition.

options.text: The electron-rich pi cloud of the alkene
options.explanation: Approaching density pushes the shared pair toward the far bromine.
The induction is intrinsic to the approach, not solvent-borne.

options.text: The hydrogen atoms on the alkene
options.explanation: Hydrogens are not the polarising agent here.

questions.stem: Which description of the polarised Br2 species is correct?

options.explanation: One atom takes the deficit, not both.
Polarisation is the entire mechanism's trigger.

options.text: Near bromine delta-positive, far bromine delta-negative
options.explanation: Electron density is pushed away from the approaching atom.

options.text: Near bromine delta-negative, far bromine delta-positive
options.explanation: The push runs away from the alkene, so the near end is positive.

questions.stem: What is the organic product when bromine adds to ethene?

options.explanation: Two bromine atoms enter; both must appear in the product.
No oxygen participates in bromine addition.
Carbon count is unchanged at two.
One bromine on each alkene carbon - di-substituted.

questions.stem: How does the Br-Br bond break during electrophilic addition to ethene?

options.text: Heterolytically, giving Br(-) and the polarised electrophile
options.explanation: Both electrons leave with the departing bromide.
Radical chemistry belongs to UV substitution routes.
Both atoms join the product, so the bond must break first.
The departing species carries one electron pair, making a single negative ion.

questions.stem: Why does the bromine water test also work through this mechanism?

options.explanation: The test works in the dark with alkenes.

options.text: The alkene induces the same dipole and consumes Br2 into a dibromo product, bleaching the reagent
options.explanation: Consumption of bromine is the visible endpoint.

options.text: Bromine water is ionic and reacts by substitution
options.explanation: The addition pathway, not substitution, consumes the reagent.
Water is the solvent; manganate does the oxidising.

questions.stem: Define an induced dipole in the context of bromine addition.
questions.modelAnswer: An induced dipole is the temporary charge separation created when the alkene's electron density pushes the Br-Br shared pair toward the far bromine, making the near atom delta-positive.

questions.stem: State the equation for bromine adding to ethene, with the product name.
questions.modelAnswer: CH2=CH2 + Br2 -> CH2BrCH2Br, the addition giving 1,2-dibromoethane.

questions.stem: Explain why bromine, though non-polar, still participates in electrophilic addition.
questions.modelAnswer: Electrophilic character does not require a permanent dipole: the pi cloud induces one on approach, and the induced delta-positive bromine behaves exactly like any other electrophile.

questions.stem: Propene is treated with bromine water. Name the organic product and state the observation.
questions.modelAnswer: Addition places bromine across the double bond to give 1,2-dibromopropane, and the orange bromine water decolourises as the reagent is consumed.
